summaries.example: Imagine a sentence saying, “These two blocks cannot occupy the very same space at the same time.” Chatton would ask what things must be real for that sentence to be true. He thought that blocks, their qualities, and something called quantity might all be needed. Ockham might try to explain the sentence with fewer kinds of things.
summaries.summary: Walter Chatton was an English philosopher and theologian who lived around 1290–1343. He studied and taught in the lively world of medieval Oxford and became a strong critic of William of Ockham. Chatton was interested in a basic question: what must be real for our true statements to be true? Ockham often favored simpler explanations with fewer entities. Chatton thought this could leave out important real things. His “Chatton Principle” said that if a true statement cannot be explained by the things already admitted, we should add what is needed. He used this approach to defend real relations and different kinds of things, while also supporting parts of Scotus’s philosophy. Chatton argued about universals, which are general ideas such as humanity, and about individual properties that make one person different from another. He also defended a difficult view about indivisibles and continuous things, especially when thinking about how angels might move. On future events, he tried to explain how God could grasp a future possibility without forcing it to happen. Chatton’s criticisms were important partly because they helped Ockham change some of his own views.
key_ideas: Walter Chatton was a fourteenth-century English philosopher and theologian who taught at Oxford and debated William of Ockham.
Chatton believed that some real structures, such as relations and quantities, were needed to explain truths about the world.
His Chatton Principle said that we should accept as many things as are needed to make a true statement true.
Chatton defended some ideas linked to John Duns Scotus, including natures and individual properties.
He also argued about whether smooth things like motion and space contain indivisible parts.
His disagreements with Ockham influenced Ockham’s later thinking about concepts and other philosophical questions.
summaries.why_it_matters: Chatton shows that philosophy grows through disagreement. He did not simply build one giant system. Instead, he tested ideas about reality, language, motion, knowledge, and choice. His debates help us see why a simple explanation can be useful but may also leave questions unanswered. They also show how medieval philosophy joined religious questions with careful arguments about logic and the world.

important_terms.definition: A philosopher who studies what kinds of things are real.
A rule about which things we must say exist in order to make a true statement true.
The idea that we should not add extra kinds of things unless they are needed.
A real individual thing, such as a person or a particular object.

questions_to_think_about: Should we always prefer an explanation with fewer kinds of things?
Can a true sentence tell us something about what exists?
What is the difference between thinking about a thing and judging that a claim about it is true?

summaries.example: Suppose the true claim is: “Two consecrated hosts cannot naturally occupy exactly the same spatial arrangement at the same time.” Chatton argues that substances and qualities alone do not explain this. Qualities can overlap, and the relevant extended bread substance is absent in the theological case he considers. He therefore argues that quantity must be admitted as a distinct kind of entity. The example illustrates his two-stage method: identify what would make the proposition true, then test whether the proposed entities are sufficient.
summaries.summary: Walter Chatton was a fourteenth-century English Franciscan philosopher and theologian whose work developed through sustained criticism of William of Ockham. Chatton was more sympathetic than Ockham to realist metaphysics, especially to the Scotistic view that reality includes structures not reducible to individual substances and their qualities. His best-known contribution is the principle later called the Chatton Principle. In one form, it says that when an affirmative proposition is true and the entities already considered could not suffice to make it true, another entity must be posited. The principle depends on a theory of truth-makers: propositions can guide ontology because things, rather than merely words, make them true. Chatton also holds that changes between contradictory states require a real basis, although Ockham expands this idea by allowing motion and time, as well as generation or destruction, to explain changes in truth. This limits the anti-razor’s force against Ockham’s semantic theory. In the theory of categories, Chatton occupies a middle position. Categories are semantic structures of concepts and terms, but they correspond to ten basic classes of real things. In the debate over universals, he follows Scotus in distinguishing repeatable natures from the individual properties that make them singular in particular beings. Chatton’s defense of indivisibles responds to Aristotelian arguments about continuous magnitudes. He denies that discrete, independently existing atoms compose continua, but allows indivisibles in potentiality within continua and gives theological reasons for rejecting unrestricted infinite divisibility. key_ideas: Chatton combined Scotistic realist commitments with close attention to logic and language, often using ideas associated with Ockham against Ockham’s conclusions.
His anti-razor is not simply a demand to add entities freely: it asks whether a given set of entities could make a known true proposition false under the relevant conditions.
He held that the ten Aristotelian categories correspond to ten basic classes of things, while also treating categories as ordered systems of concepts or terms.
In the debate over universals, Chatton defended individuated natures together with individual properties rather than reducing everything to radically particular entities.
His indivisibilism was aimed mainly at physical and theological problems, such as angelic motion, rather than at constructing a modern mathematical theory of continua.
Regarding future contingents, Chatton challenged the claim that God’s certain knowledge makes future events necessary by distinguishing divine cognition from judgmental knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: Chatton is important as a case study in how medieval philosophy connects metaphysics, logic, language, theology, and natural philosophy. His arguments clarify a recurring issue: when does a successful explanation require new entities, and when does it merely reflect a misleading analysis of language? His influence on Ockham also demonstrates that philosophical disagreement can change an opponent’s position rather than simply produce winners and losers.

important_terms.definition: The question of what a statement or theory commits us to as existing.
A principle of explanatory economy that resists adding entities without sufficient reason; it is associated with Ockham, though the familiar slogan is not his precise formulation.
Chatton’s rule that reality must include whatever entities are required to make a true affirmative proposition true, under specified conditions.
A thing or entity considered as something existing outside the mind.
A general nature or property that can be instantiated by more than one individual, such as humanity, though Chatton holds that it exists outside the mind only in individuated form.
An individual property, often called a haecceity, that makes a particular instance uniquely that individual.
The view that continuous magnitudes can be analyzed using indivisible entities, especially in physical and theological contexts.
Chatton’s distinction between merely grasping a thing and affirmatively judging or assenting to a proposition about it.

questions_to_think_about: Does a true proposition by itself establish that a particular kind of entity exists? What further assumptions are needed?
Can a theory be both realist about some entities and strongly attentive to semantics and logic?
Does Chatton’s treatment of indivisibles answer Aristotle’s argument, or mainly restrict the argument’s relevance?
Can direct cognition of a future contingent preserve contingency without making divine awareness incomplete?

summaries.example: Imagine your class has a true rule: “A red ball and a blue ball cannot be in exactly the same place at the same moment.” One student says the balls and their colors explain the rule. Chatton might ask whether those things are enough. He could argue that another feature—quantity, which concerns size or spatial impenetrability—is needed. Ockham might reply that movement, time, or the way the sentence is understood could explain the difference without adding another entity.
summaries.summary: Walter Chatton was an English philosopher and theologian of the early fourteenth century. He worked in the intellectual setting of Oxford and became one of William of Ockham’s strongest critics. Chatton also drew on John Duns Scotus, so his philosophy combined realist ideas with careful attention to language and logic. A major issue between Chatton and Ockham was ontology: deciding what kinds of things really exist. Ockham is associated with a parsimonious approach, often explained through the image of a razor. Chatton worried that this approach could explain away things that were genuinely needed. His Chatton Principle says that when a true affirmative statement cannot be made true by the entities already under consideration, another entity must be admitted. He used this method to argue for real relations and for different kinds of things behind Aristotle’s ten categories. Chatton thought categories were systems of concepts and terms, but also matched ten basic classes of real entities. In the debate over universals, he defended the idea that individuals contain natures, such as humanity, together with individual properties that make each nature belong to one particular person. He also defended indivisibilism in certain physical and theological discussions, especially questions about continuous motion and angels. Finally, he addressed future contingents. A fatalist argument says that if God infallibly knows a future event, that event must be necessary. Chatton challenged this by distinguishing God’s direct cognition of a future thing from judgmental knowledge that would determine its existence. His work also influenced Ockham’s later theory of concepts.
key_ideas: Chatton and Ockham disagreed about whether philosophy should admit extra kinds of entities to explain true statements.
Chatton’s principle says that if the things already accepted cannot make a true claim true, we should posit another thing.
Chatton believed categories describe both kinds of terms and kinds of real things, placing him between Scotus and Ockham.
He defended a view in which general natures, such as humanity, are present in individuals in an individualized way and are universal in the mind.
His arguments about indivisibles were connected to questions about continuous motion, space, time, and angelic movement.
He tried to avoid fatalism by saying that God’s grasp of a future event need not make that event necessary.
summaries.why_it_matters: Chatton matters because he shows philosophy as an active exchange of objections and replies. His arguments raise questions that still appear today: what does language tell us about reality, when should we add hidden structures to an explanation, and how can knowledge of the future fit with genuine alternatives? His career also shows how medieval thinkers used religious frameworks while debating logic, mind, motion, and the structure of the world.

important_terms.definition: A view about what exists and what kinds of things are real.
A rule for deciding what kinds of things must exist to make a true claim true.
The strategy of avoiding unnecessary additions to an explanation.
A general idea or property that can apply to many individuals, such as being human.
A particular feature that makes one individual distinct from others of the same kind.
The view that smooth things such as space, time, or motion may involve indivisible units.
A future event that could happen but could also fail to happen.
A mental act that changes the soul or mind, rather than a separate object inside the mind.

questions_to_think_about: Is a simpler theory always better, or can it leave out something important?
How could one idea, such as humanity, relate to many different people?
Why might a philosopher use a theological example to argue about space or quantity?
What is the difference between knowing that something will happen and merely grasping it as a possibility?
